variants.name: Typed Node streams with write()/drain and pipeline()
variants.implementation_notes: TypeScript adds no runtime mechanism, but it makes the handshake checkable: Node's Readable/Writable interfaces are typed (write(chunk): boolean, the 'drain' event, pipeline() from node:stream/promises) and `for await (const chunk of readable)` is demand-driven, so the classic bounded queue is replaced by the platform's buffering plus a signal the compiler can help you not to discard. The typed surface is the point: a boolean return that is ignored compiles, so the discipline lives in code review and tests rather than in the type system. Where the pipeline is described declaratively, pipeline() with an async-generator transform keeps the whole chain paced by the slowest writable.
pitfalls: TypeScript will not force you to await 'drain' after a false write(): the boolean is easy to discard and the bug ships.
Readable.from() over an array or generator loses pacing if the source is a hot producer that ignores the consumer's readiness.
Mixing node:stream and Web Streams needs explicit adapters (Readable.fromWeb/toWeb) and the handshake does not survive automatically.
Typing a buffer as Buffer[] and accumulating chunks in the consumer re-creates an unbounded queue in memory.

variants.name: Typed Web Streams pull source with a queuing strategy
variants.implementation_notes: The Web Streams realization is declarative: a ReadableStream is constructed with an underlying pull() source and a queuing strategy (CountQueuingStrategy/ByteLengthQueuingStrategy with a highWaterMark), and the platform calls pull only while the queue has room, exposing ReadableStreamDefaultController.desiredSize as the remaining capacity. TypeScript types the strategy and the controller, so the bound is visible in the type signature rather than hidden in a runtime option. The classic queue is replaced by the strategy object; a source that ignores desiredSize (or enqueues outside pull) has no bound at all.
pitfalls: desiredSize is remaining capacity, not a size to fill: negative values mean the queue is over the high-water mark and the source must stop.
Implementing the source with a background producer that enqueues regardless of pull() removes the bound the strategy was meant to give.
Transporting a ReadableStream across a boundary (worker, fetch body) requires a reader on the other side, or the stream is never pulled and buffers indefinitely.
Web Streams are asynchronous by definition; sharing the same stream with two consumers splits the data - use tee() and expect both branches to be consumed.
